entries.c8abe72ecf2981daf08d074d5e817a1f67bbb76e: <div sID="gen9715" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="20" osisID="Job.20" sID="Job.20"/> <div eID="gen9715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9716" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9717" type="x-p"/> One would have thought that such an excellent confession of faith as Job made, in the close of the foregoing chapter, would satisfy his friends, or at least mollify them; but they do not seem to have taken any notice of it, and therefore Zophar here takes his turn, enters the lists with Job, and attacks him with as much vehemence as before. I. His preface is short, but hot, <reference osisRef="Job.20.2-Job.20.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. II. His discourse is long, and all upon one subject, the very same that Bildad was large upon (<reference osisRef="Job.18.1-Job.18.21">ch. xviii.</reference>), the certain misery of wicked people and the ruin that awaits them. 1. He asserts, in general, that the prosperity of a wicked person is short, and his ruin sure, <reference osisRef="Job.20.4-Job.20.9">ver. 4-9</reference>. 2. He proves the misery of his condition by many instances—that he should have a diseased body, a troubled conscience, a ruined estate, a beggared family, an infamous name and that he himself should perish under the weight of divine wrath: all this is most curiously described here in lofty expressions and lively similitudes; and it often proves true in this world, and always in another, without repentance, <reference osisRef="Job.20.10-Job.20.29">ver. 10-29</reference>. But the great mistake was, and (as bishop Patrick expresses it) all the flaw in his discourse (which was common to him with the rest), that he imagined God never varied from this method, and therefore Job was, without doubt, a very bad man, though it did not appear that he was, any other way than by his infelicity.
entries.3091b0677785c323554c1e86fe9c53a0001a0bde: <div eID="gen9717" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9716" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Second Address of Zophar; Destruction of the Wicked. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9718" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said, 2 Therefore do my thoughts cause me to answer, and for <hi type="italic">this</hi> I make haste. <hi type="super">3</hi> I have heard the check of my reproach, and the spirit of my understanding causeth me to answer. 4 Knowest thou <hi type="italic">not</hi> this of old, since man was placed upon earth, <hi type="super">5</hi> That the triumphing of the wicked <hi type="italic">is</hi> short, and the joy of the hypocrite <hi type="italic">but</hi> for a moment? <hi type="super">6</hi> Though his excellency mount up to the heavens, and his head reach unto the clouds; <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="italic">Yet</hi> he shall perish for ever like his own dung: they which have seen him shall say, Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> he? <hi type="super">8</hi> He shall fly away as a dream, and shall not be found: yea, he shall be chased away as a vision of the night. <hi type="super">9</hi> The eye also <hi type="italic">which</hi> saw him shall <hi type="italic">see him</hi> no more; neither shall his place any more behold him. <div eID="gen9718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9719" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Zophar begins very passionately, and seems to be in a great heat at what Job had said. Being resolved to condemn Job for a bad man, he was much displeased that he talked so like a good man, and, as it should seem, broke in upon him, and began abruptly (<reference osisRef="Job.20.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore do my thoughts cause me to answer.</hi> He takes no notice of what Job had said to move their pity, or to evidence his own integrity, but fastens upon the reproof he gave them in the close of his discourse, counts that a reproach, and thinks himself <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> obliged to answer, because Job had bidden them be afraid of the sword, that he might not seem to be frightened by his menaces. The best counsel is too often ill taken from an antagonist, and therefore usually may be well spared. Zophar seemed more in haste to speak than became a wise man; but he excuses his haste with two things:—1. That Job had given him strong provocation (<reference osisRef="Job.20.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have heard the check of my reproach,</hi> and cannot bear to hear it any longer." Job's friends, I doubt, had spirits too high to deal with a man in his low condition; and high spirits are impatient of contradiction, and think themselves affronted if all about them do not say as they say; they cannot bear a check but they call it <hi type="italic">the check of their reproach,</hi> and then they are bound in honour to return it, if not to draw upon him that gave it. 2. That his own heart gave him a strong instigation. His thoughts caused him to answer (<reference osisRef="Job.20.2">v. 2</reference>), for <hi type="italic">out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks;</hi> but he fathers the instigation (<reference osisRef="Job.20.3">v. 3</reference>) upon <hi type="italic">the spirit of his understanding:</hi> that indeed should cause us to answer; we should rightly apprehend a thing and duly consider it before we speak of it; but whether it did so here or no is a question. Men often mistake the dictates of their passion for the dictates of their reason, and therefore think they do well to be angry. <div eID="gen9719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9720" type="x-p"/> II. Zophar proceeds very plainly to show the ruin and destruction of wicked people, insinuating that because Job was destroyed and ruined he was certainly a wicked man and a hypocrite. Observe, <div eID="gen9720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9721" type="x-p"/> 1. How this doctrine is introduced, <reference osisRef="Job.20.4">v. 4</reference>, where he appeals, (1.) To Job's own knowledge and conviction: "<hi type="italic">Knowest thou not this?</hi> Canst thou be ignorant of a truth so plain? Or canst thou doubt of a truth which has been confirmed by the suffrages of all mankind?" Those know little who do not know that the wages of sin is death. (2.) To the experience of all ages. It was known of old, since man was placed upon the earth; that is, ever since man was made he has had this truth written in his heart, that the sin of sinners will be their ruin; and ever since there were instances of wickedness (which there were soon after man was placed on the earth) there were instances of the punishments of it, witness the exclusions of Adam and Cain. When sin entered into the world death entered with it: all the world knows that evil pursues sinners, whom <hi type="italic">vengeance suffers not to live</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.4">Acts xxviii. 4</reference>), and subscribes to that (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.11">Isa. iii. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Woe to the wicked; it shall be ill with him,</hi> sooner or later. <div eID="gen9721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9722" type="x-p"/> 2. How it is laid down (<reference osisRef="Job.20.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The triumphing of the wicked is short, and the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment.</hi> Observe, (1.) He asserts the misery, not only of those who are openly wicked and profane, but of hypocrites, who secretly practice wickedness under a show and profession of religion, because such a wicked man he looked upon Job to be; and it is true that a form of godliness, if it be made use of for a cloak of maliciousness, does but make bad worse. Dissembled piety is double iniquity, and the ruin that attends it will be accordingly. The hottest place in hell will be the portion of hypocrites, as our Saviour intimates, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.51">Matt. xxiv. 51</reference>. (2.) He grants that wicked men may for a time prosper, may be secure and easy, and very merry. You may see them in triumph and joy, triumphing and rejoicing in their wealth and power, their grandeur and success, triumphing and rejoicing over their poor honest neighbours whom they vex and oppress: they feel no evil, they fear none. Job's friends were loth to own, at first, that wicked people might prosper at all (<reference osisRef="Job.4.9">ch. iv. 9</reference>), until Job proved it plainly (<reference osisRef="Job.9.24">ch. ix. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.12.6">xii. 6</reference>), and now Zophar yields it; but, (3.) He lays it down for a certain truth that they will not prosper long. Their joy is but for a moment, and will quickly end in endless sorrow. Though he be ever so great, and rich, and jovial, the hypocrite will be humbled, and mortified, and made miserable. <div eID="gen9722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9723" type="x-p"/> 3. How it is illustrated, <reference osisRef="Job.20.6-Job.20.9">v. 6-9</reference>. (1.) He supposes his prosperity to be very high, as high as you can imagine, <reference osisRef="Job.20.6">v. 6</reference>. It is not his wisdom and virtue, but his worldly wealth or greatness, that he accounts <hi type="italic">his excellency,</hi> and values himself upon. We will suppose that <hi type="italic">to mount up to the heavens,</hi> and, since his spirit always rises with his condition, you may suppose that with it <hi type="italic">his head reaches to the clouds.</hi> He is every way advanced; the world has done the utmost it can for him. He looks down upon all about him with disdain, while they look up to him with admiration, envy, or fear. We will suppose him to bid fair for a universal monarchy. And, though he cannot but have made himself many enemies before he arrived to this pitch of prosperity, yet he thinks himself as much out of the reach of their darts as if he were in the clouds. (2.) He is confident that his ruin will accordingly be very great, and his fall the more dreadful for his having risen so high: <hi type="italic">He shall perish for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.20.7">v. 7</reference>. His pride and security were the certain presages of his misery. This will certainly be true of all impenitent sinners in the other world; they shall be undone, for ever undone. But Zophar means his ruin in this world; and indeed sometimes notorious sinners are remarkably cut off by present judgments; they have reason enough to fear what Zophar here threatens even the triumphant sinner with. [1.] A shameful destruction: <hi type="italic">He shall perish like his own dung</hi> or dunghill, so loathsome is he to God and all good men, and so willing will the world be to part with him, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.119">Ps. cxix. 119</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.24">Isa. lxvi. 24</reference>. [2.] A surprising destruction. He will be brought into desolation in a moment (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.19">Ps. lxxiii. 19</reference>), so that those about him, that saw him but just now, will ask, "<hi type="italic">Where is he?</hi> Could he that made so great a figure vanish and expire so suddenly?" [3.] A swift destruction, <reference osisRef="Job.20.8">v. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">He shall fly away</hi> upon the wings of his own terrors, and be <hi type="italic">chased away</hi> by the just imprecations of all about him, who would gladly get rid of him. [4.] An utter destruction. It will be total; he shall go away <hi type="italic">like a dream,</hi> or <hi type="italic">vision of the night,</hi> which was a mere phantasm, and, whatever in it pleased the fancy, it is quite gone, and nothing of it remains but what serves us to laugh at the folly of. It will be final (<reference osisRef="Job.20.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">The eye that saw him,</hi> and was ready to adore him, <hi type="italic">shall see him no more,</hi> and the place he filled shall no more behold him, having given him an eternal farewell when he went to his own place, as Judas, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.25">Acts i. 25</reference>.
entries.17e1ec15bcfddaf9de44059192178baf1159b940: <div eID="gen9723" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Misery of the Wicked. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9724" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> His children shall seek to please the poor, and his hands shall restore their goods. <hi type="super">11</hi> His bones are full <hi type="italic">of the sin</hi> of his youth, which shall lie down with him in the dust. <hi type="super">12</hi> Though wickedness be sweet in his mouth, <hi type="italic">though</hi> he hide it under his tongue; <hi type="super">13</hi> <hi type="italic">Though</hi> he spare it, and forsake it not; but keep it still within his mouth: <hi type="super">14</hi> <hi type="italic">Yet</hi> his meat in his bowels is turned, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> the gall of asps within him. <hi type="super">15</hi> He hath swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again: God shall cast them out of his belly. <hi type="super">16</hi> He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him. <hi type="super">17</hi> He shall not see the rivers, the floods, the brooks of honey and butter. <hi type="super">18</hi> That which he laboured for shall he restore, and shall not swallow <hi type="italic">it</hi> down: according to <hi type="italic">his</hi> substance <hi type="italic">shall</hi> the restitution <hi type="italic">be,</hi> and he shall not rejoice <hi type="italic">therein.</hi> 19 Because he hath oppressed <hi type="italic">and</hi> hath forsaken the poor; <hi type="italic">because</hi> he hath violently taken away a house which he builded not; <hi type="super">20</hi> Surely he shall not feel quietness in his belly, he shall not save of that which he desired. <hi type="super">21</hi> There shall none of his meat be left; therefore shall no man look for his goods. <hi type="super">22</hi> In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits: every hand of the wicked shall come upon him. <div eID="gen9724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9725" type="x-p"/> The instances here given of the miserable condition of the wicked man in this world are expressed with great fulness and fluency of language, and the same thing returned to again and repeated in other words. Let us therefore reduce the particulars to their proper heads, and observe, <div eID="gen9725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9726" type="x-p"/> I. What his wickedness is for which he is punished. <div eID="gen9726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9727" type="x-p"/> 1. The lusts of the flesh, here called <hi type="italic">the sins of his youth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.11">v. 11</reference>); for those are the sins which, at that age, people are most tempted to. The forbidden pleasures of sense are said to be <hi type="italic">sweet in his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.12">v. 12</reference>); he indulges himself in all the gratifications of the carnal appetite, and takes an inordinate complacency in them, as yielding the most agreeable delights. That is the satisfaction which <hi type="italic">he hides under his tongue,</hi> and rolls there, as the most dainty delicate thing that can be. <hi type="italic">He keeps it still within his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.13">v. 13</reference>); let him have that, and he desires no more; he will never part with that for the spiritual and divine pleasures of religion, which he has no relish or nor affection for. His keeping it still in his mouth denotes his obstinately persisting in his sin (<hi type="italic">he spares it</hi> when he should kill and mortify it, <hi type="italic">and forsakes it not,</hi> but holds it fast, and goes on frowardly in it), and also his re-acting of his sin by revolving it and remembering it with pleasure, as that adulterous woman (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.19">Ezek. xxiii. 19</reference>) who <hi type="italic">multiplied her whoredoms by calling to remembrance the days of her youth;</hi> so does this wicked man here. Or his hiding it and keeping it under his tongue denotes his industrious concealment of his beloved lust. Being a hypocrite, his haunts of sin are secret, that he may save the credit of his profession; but he who knows what is in the heart knows what is under the tongue too, and will discover it shortly. <div eID="gen9727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9728" type="x-p"/> 2. The love of the world and the wealth of it. It is in worldly wealth that he places his happiness, and therefore he sets his heart upon it. See here, (1.) How greedy he is of it (<reference osisRef="Job.20.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">He has swallowed down riches</hi> as eagerly as ever a hungry man swallowed down meat; and is still crying, "Give, give." It is that which he desired (<reference osisRef="Job.20.20">v. 20</reference>); it was, in his eye, the best gift, and that which he coveted earnestly. (2.) What pains he takes for it: It is <hi type="italic">that which he laboured for</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.18">v. 18</reference>), not by honest diligence in a lawful calling, but by an unwearied prosecution of all ways and methods, <hi type="italic">per fas, per nefas—right or wrong,</hi> to be rich. We must <hi type="italic">labour,</hi> not <hi type="italic">to be rich</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.4">Prov. xxiii. 4</reference>), but to be charitable, <hi type="italic">that we may have to give</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Eph. iv. 28</reference>), not to spend. (3.) What great things he promises himself from it, intimated in <hi type="italic">the rivers, the floods, the brooks of honey and butter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.17">v. 17</reference>); his being disappointed of them supposes that he had flattered himself with the hopes of them: he expected rivers of sensual delights. <div eID="gen9728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9729" type="x-p"/> 3. Violence and oppression, and injustice in his poor neighbours, <reference osisRef="Job.20.19">v. 19</reference>. This was the sin of the giants of the old world, and a sin that, as much as any, brings God's judgments upon nations and families. It is charged upon this wicked man, (1.) That <hi type="italic">he has forsaken the poor,</hi> taken no care of them, shown no kindness to them, nor made any provision for them. At first perhaps, for a pretence, he gave alms like the Pharisees, to gain a reputation; but, when he had served his turn by this practice, he left it off, and forsook the poor, whom before he seemed to be concerned for. Those who do good, but not from a good principle, though they may abound in it, will not abide in it. (2.) That he has <hi type="italic">oppressed</hi> them, crushed them, taken all advantages against them to do them a mischief. To enrich himself, he has robbed the spital, and made the poor poorer. (3.) That he has <hi type="italic">violently taken away their houses,</hi> which he had no right to, as Ahab took Naboth's vineyard, not by secret fraud, by forgery, perjury, or some trick in law, but avowedly, and by open violence. <div eID="gen9729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9730" type="x-p"/> II. What his punishment is for this wickedness. <div eID="gen9730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9731" type="x-p"/> 1. He shall be disappointed in his expectations, and shall not find that satisfaction in his worldly wealth which he vainly promised himself (<reference osisRef="Job.20.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall never see the rivers, the floods, the brooks of honey and butter,</hi> with which he hoped to glut himself. The world is not that to those who love it, and court it, and admire it, which they fancy it will be. The enjoyment sinks far below the raised expectation. <div eID="gen9731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9732" type="x-p"/> 2. He shall be diseased and distempered in his body; and how little comfort a man has in riches if he has not health! Sickness and pain, especially it they be in extremity, embitter all his enjoyments. This wicked man has all the delights of sense wound up to the height of pleasurableness; but what real happiness can he enjoy when <hi type="italic">his bones are full of the sins of his youth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.11">v. 11</reference>), that is, of the effects of those sins? By his drunkenness and gluttony, his uncleanness and wantonness, when he was young, he contracted those diseases which are painful to him long after, and perhaps make his life very miserable, and, as Solomon speaks, consume his flesh and his body, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.11">Prov. v. 11</reference>. Perhaps he was given to fight when he was young, and then made nothing of a cut or a bruise in a fray; but he feels it in his bones long after. But can he get no ease, no relief? No, he is likely to carry his pains and diseases with him to the grave, or rather they are likely to carry him thither, and so the sins of his youth shall <hi type="italic">lie down with him in the dust;</hi> the very putrefying of his body in the grave is to him the effect of sin (<reference osisRef="Job.24.19">ch. xxiv. 19</reference>), so that his iniquity is upon his bones there, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.27">Ezek. xxxii. 27</reference>. The sin of sinners follows them to the other side death. <div eID="gen9732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9733" type="x-p"/> 3. He shall be disquieted and troubled in his mind: <hi type="italic">Surely he shall not feel quietness in his belly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.20.20">v. 20</reference>. He has not that ease in his own mind that people think he has, but is in continual agitation. The ill-gotten wealth which he has swallowed down makes him sick, and, like undigested meat, is always upbraiding him. Let none expect to enjoy that comfortably which they have gotten unjustly. The unquietness of his mind arises, (1.) From his conscience looking back, and filling him with the fear of the wrath of God against him for his wickedness. Even that wickedness which was sweet in the commission, and was rolled under the tongue as a delicate morsel, becomes bitter in the reflection, and, when it is reviewed, fills him with horror and vexation. <hi type="italic">In his bowels it is turned</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.14">v. 14</reference>) like John's book, <hi type="italic">in his mouth as sweet as honey,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">when he had eaten it, his belly was bitter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.10.10">Rev. x. 10</reference>. Such a thing is sin; it is turned into <hi type="italic">the gall of asps,</hi> than which nothing is more bitter, <hi type="italic">the poison of asps</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.16">v. 16</reference>), than which nothing more fatal, and so it will be to him; what he sucked so sweetly, and with so much pleasure, will prove to him the poison of asps; so will all unlawful gains be. The fawning tongue will prove the viper's tongue. All the charming graces that are thought to be in sin will, when conscience is awakened, turn into so many raging furies. (2.) From his cares, looking forward, <reference osisRef="Job.20.22">v. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">In the fulness of his sufficiency,</hi> when he thinks himself most happy, and most sure of the continuance of his happiness, <hi type="italic">he shall be in straits,</hi> that is, he shall think himself so, through the anxieties and perplexities of his own mind, as that rich man who, when his ground brought forth plentifully, cried out, <hi type="italic">What shall I do?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.17">Luke xii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen9733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9734" type="x-p"/> 4. He shall be dispossessed of his estate; that shall sink and dwindle away to nothing, so that <hi type="italic">he shall not rejoice therein,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.20.18">v. 18</reference>. He shall not only never rejoice truly, but not long rejoice at all. (1.) What he has unjustly swallowed he shall be compelled to disgorge (<reference osisRef="Job.20.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">He swallowed down riches,</hi> and then thought himself sure of them, and that they were as much his own as the meat he had eaten; but he was deceived: <hi type="italic">he shall vomit them up again;</hi> his own conscience perhaps may make him so uneasy in the keeping of what he has gotten that, for the quiet of his own mind, he shall make restitution, and that not with the pleasure of a virtue, but the pain of a vomit, and with the utmost reluctancy. Or, if he do not himself refund what he has violently taken away, God will, by his providence, force him to it, and bring it about, one way or other, that ill-gotten goods shall return to the right owners: <hi type="italic">God shall cast them out of his belly,</hi> while yet the love of the sin is not cast out of his heart. So loud shall the clamours of the poor, whom he has impoverished, be against him, that he shall be forced to send his children to them to soothe them and beg their pardon (<reference osisRef="Job.20.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">His children shall seek to please the poor,</hi> while his own hands shall restore them their goods with shame (<reference osisRef="Job.20.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">That which he laboured for,</hi> by all the arts of oppression, <hi type="italic">shall he restore,</hi> and shall not so swallow it down as to digest it; it shall not stay with him, but <hi type="italic">according to his shame shall the restitution be;</hi> having gotten a great deal unjustly, he shall restore a great deal, so that when every one has his own he will have but little left for himself. To be made to restore what was unjustly gotten, by the sanctifying grace of God, as Zaccheus was, is a great mercy; he voluntarily and cheerfully restored four-fold, and yet had a great deal left to <hi type="italic">give to the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.8">Luke xix. 8</reference>. But to be forced to restore, as Judas was, merely by the horrors of a despairing conscience, has none of that benefit and comfort attending it, for he <hi type="italic">threw down the pieces of silver and went and hanged himself.</hi> (2.) He shall be stripped of all he has and become a beggar. He that spoiled others shall himself be spoiled (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa. xxxiii. 1</reference>); for <hi type="italic">every hand of the wicked shall be upon him.</hi> The innocent, whom he has wronged, sit down by their loss, saying, as David, <hi type="italic">Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked, but my hand shall not be upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.13">1 Sam. xxiv. 13</reference>. But though they have forgiven him, though they will make no reprisals, divine justice will, and often makes the wicked to avenge the quarrel of the righteous, and squeezes and crushes one bad man by the hand of another upon him. Thus, when he is plucked on all sides, <hi type="italic">he shall not save of that which he desired</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.20">v. 20</reference>), not only he shall not save it all, but he shall save nothing of it. <hi type="italic">There shall none of his meat</hi> (which he coveted so much, and fed upon with so much pleasure) <hi type="italic">be left,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.20.21">v. 21</reference>. All his neighbours and relations shall look upon him to be in such bad circumstances that, when he is dead, no man shall look for his goods, none of his kindred shall expect to be a penny the better for him, nor be willing to take out letters of administration for what he leaves behind him. In all this Zophar reflects upon Job, who had lost all and was reduced to the last extremity.
entries.7802549f8100a65c859a3c7319b241621b15d468: <div eID="gen9734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9735" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> <hi type="italic">When</hi> he is about to fill his belly, <hi type="italic">God</hi> shall cast the fury of his wrath upon him, and shall rain <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon him while he is eating. <hi type="super">24</hi> He shall flee from the iron weapon, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the bow of steel shall strike him through. <hi type="super">25</hi> It is drawn, and cometh out of the body; yea, the glittering sword cometh out of his gall: terrors <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon him. <hi type="super">26</hi> All darkness <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> hid in his secret places: a fire not blown shall consume him; it shall go ill with him that is left in his tabernacle. <hi type="super">27</hi> The heaven shall reveal his iniquity; and the earth shall rise up against him. 28 The increase of his house shall depart, <hi type="italic">and his goods</hi> shall flow away in the day of his wrath. <hi type="super">29</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the portion of a wicked man from God, and the heritage appointed unto him by God. <div eID="gen9735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9736" type="x-p"/> Zophar, having described the many embarrassments and vexations which commonly attend the wicked practices of oppressors and cruel men, here comes to show their utter ruin at last. <div eID="gen9736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9737" type="x-p"/> I. Their ruin will take its rise from God's wrath and vengeance, <reference osisRef="Job.20.23">v. 23</reference>. The hand of the wicked was upon him (<reference osisRef="Job.20.22">v. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">every hand of the wicked.</hi> His hand was against every one, and therefore every man's hand will be against him. Yet, in grappling with these, he might go near to make his part good; but his heart cannot endure, nor his hands be strong, when <hi type="italic">God shall deal with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.14">Ezek. xxii. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">when God shall cast the fury of his wrath upon him and rain it upon him.</hi> Every word here speaks terror. It is not only the justice of God that is engaged against him, but his wrath, the deep resentment of provocations given to himself; it is <hi type="italic">the fury of his wrath,</hi> incensed to the highest degree; it is cast upon him with force and fierceness; it is rained upon him in abundance; it comes on his head like the fire and brimstone upon Sodom, to which the psalmist also refers, <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Ps. xi. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">On the wicked God shall rain fire and brimstone.</hi> There is no fence against this, but in Christ, who is the only covert from the storm and tempest, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa. xxxii. 2</reference>. This wrath shall be cast upon him <hi type="italic">when he is about to fill his belly,</hi> just going to glut himself with what he has gotten and promising himself abundant satisfaction in it. Then, when he is eating, shall this tempest surprise him, when he is secure and easy, and in apprehension of no danger; as the ruin of the old world and Sodom came when they were in the depth of their security and the height of their sensuality, as Christ observes, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.26-Luke.17.31">Luke xvii. 26</reference>, &c. Perhaps Zophar here reflects on the death of Job's children when they were eating and drinking. <div eID="gen9737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9738" type="x-p"/> II. Their ruin will be inevitable, and there will be no possibility of escaping it (<reference osisRef="Job.20.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall flee from the iron weapon.</hi> Flight argues guilt. He will not humble himself under the judgments of God, nor seek means to make his peace with him. All his care is to escape the vengeance that pursues him, but in vain: if he escape the sword, yet <hi type="italic">the bow of steel shall strike him through.</hi> God has weapons of all sorts; he has both <hi type="italic">whet his sword and bent his bow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.12-Ps.7.13">Ps. vii. 12, 13</reference>); he can deal with his enemies <hi type="italic">cominus vel eminus—at hand or afar off.</hi> He has a sword for those that think to fight it out with him by their strength, and a bow for those that think to avoid him by their craft. See <reference osisRef="Isa.24.17-Isa.24.18">Isa. xxiv. 17, 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.43-Jer.48.44">Jer. xlviii. 43, 44</reference>. He that is marked for ruin, though he may escape one judgment, will find another ready for him. <div eID="gen9738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9739" type="x-p"/> III. It will be a total terrible ruin. When the dart that has struck him through (for when God shoots he is sure to hit his mark, when he strikes he strikes home) comes to be <hi type="italic">drawn out of his body,</hi> when <hi type="italic">the glittering sword</hi> (the <hi type="italic">lightning,</hi> so the word is), the flaming sword, the sword that is bathed in heaven (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.5">Isa. xxxiv. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">comes out of his gall,</hi> O what <hi type="italic">terrors are upon him!</hi> How strong are the convulsions, how violent are the dying agonies! How terrible are the arrests of death to a wicked man! <div eID="gen9739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9740" type="x-p"/> IV. Sometimes it is a ruin that comes upon him insensibly, <reference osisRef="Job.20.26">v. 26</reference>. 1. The darkness he is wrapped up in is a hidden darkness: it is <hi type="italic">all darkness,</hi> utter darkness, without the least mixture of light, and it is <hi type="italic">hid in his secret place,</hi> whither he has retreated and where he hopes to shelter himself; he never retires into his own conscience but he finds himself in the dark and utterly at a loss. 2. The fire he is consumed by is <hi type="italic">a fire not blown,</hi> kindled without noise, a consumption which every body sees the effect of, but nobody sees the cause of. It is plain that the gourd is withered, but the worm at the root, that causes it to wither, is out of sight. He is wasted by a soft gentle fire—surely, but very slowly. When the fuel is very combustible, the fire needs no blowing, and that is his case; he is ripe for ruin. <hi type="italic">The proud, and those that do wickedly, shall be stubble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1">Mal. iv. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">An unquenchable fire shall consume him</hi> (so some read it), and that is certainly true of hell-fire. <div eID="gen9740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9741" type="x-p"/> V. It is a ruin, not only to himself, but to his family: <hi type="italic">It shall go ill with him that is left in his tabernacle,</hi> for the curse shall reach him, and he shall be cut off perhaps by the same grievous disease. There is an entail of wrath upon the family, which will destroy both his heirs and his inheritance, <reference osisRef="Job.20.28">v. 28</reference>. 1. His posterity will be rooted out: <hi type="italic">The increase of his house shall depart,</hi> shall either be cut off by untimely deaths or forced to run their country. Numerous and growing families, if wicked and vile, are soon reduced, dispersed, and extirpated, by the judgments of God. 2. His estate will be sunk. <hi type="italic">His goods shall flow away</hi> from his family as fast as ever they flowed into it, when <hi type="italic">the day of God's wrath</hi> comes, for which, all the while his estate was in the getting by fraud and oppression, he was treasuring up wrath. <div eID="gen9741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9742" type="x-p"/> VI. It is a ruin which will manifestly appear to be just and righteous, and what he has brought upon himself by his own wickedness; for (<reference osisRef="Job.20.27">v. 27</reference>) <hi type="italic">the heaven shall reveal his iniquity,</hi> that is, the God of heaven, who sees all the secret wickedness of the wicked, will, by some means or other, let all the world know what a base man he has been, that they may own the justice of God in all that is brought upon him. <hi type="italic">The earth</hi> also <hi type="italic">shall rise up against him,</hi> both to discover his wickedness and to avenge it. <hi type="italic">The earth shall disclose her blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Isa. xxvi. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">The earth will rise up against him</hi> (as the stomach rises against that which is loathsome), and will no longer keep him. <hi type="italic">The heaven reveals his iniquity,</hi> and therefore will not receive him. Whither then must he go but to hell? If the God of heaven and earth be his enemy, neither heaven nor earth will show him any kindness, but all the hosts of both are and will be at war with him. <div eID="gen9742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9743" type="x-p"/> VII. Zophar concludes like an orator (<reference osisRef="Job.20.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">This is the portion of a wicked man from God;</hi> it is allotted him, it is designed him, as his portion. He will have it at last, as a child has his portion, and he will have it for a perpetuity; it is what he must abide by: <hi type="italic">This is the heritage of his decree from God;</hi> it is the settled rule of his judgment, and fair warning is given of it. <hi type="italic">O wicked man! thou shalt surely die,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.8">Ezek. xxxiii. 8</reference>. Though impenitent sinners do not always fall under such temporal judgments as are here described (therein Zophar was mistaken), yet the wrath of God abides upon them, and they are made miserable by spiritual judgments, which are much worse, their consciences being either, on the one hand, a terror to them, and then they are in continual amazement, or, on the other hand, seared and silenced, and then they are given up to a reprobate sense and bound over to eternal ruin. Never was any doctrine better explained, or worse applied, than this by Zophar, who intended by all this to prove Job a hypocrite. Let us receive the good explication, and make a better application, for warning to ourselves to stand in awe and not to sin.  <chapter eID="Job.20"/> <div eID="gen9743" type="x-p"/>

Therefore--</hi>Rather, the more excited I feel by Job's speech, the more for that very reason shall my reply be supplied by my calm consideration. Literally, "Notwithstanding; my calm thoughts (as in <reference osisRef="Job.4.13">Job 4:13</reference>) shall furnish my answer, because of the excitement (haste) within me" [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7144" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ec25e2047ca1cfc4f71c7843c07e55dd53b0a8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4872"/><div sID="gen7145" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4872"/><hi type="bold">3. check of my reproach--</hi>that is, the castigation intended as a reproach (literally, "shame") to me.<div eID="gen7145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spirit of ... understanding--</hi>my rational spirit; answering to "calm thoughts" (<reference osisRef="Job.20.2">Job 20:2</reference>). In spite of thy reproach urging me to "hastiness." I will answer in calm reason. <div eID="gen7146" type="x-p"/>

entries.36e3ae6c7c42f05b52f308b42281df559e6ea969: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4875"/><div sID="gen7149" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4875"/><hi type="bold">7. dung--</hi>in contrast to the haughtiness of the sinner (<reference osisRef="Job.20.6">Job 20:6</reference>); this strong term expresses disgust and the lowest degradation (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.10">Psa 83:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.10">1Ki 14:10</reference>). <div eID="gen7149" type="x-p"/>

entries.444486cc8813a4c7030adffd9640fddf9ab6173b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4877"/><div sID="gen7151" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4877"/>9. Rather "the eye followeth him, but can discern him no more." A sharp-looking is meant (<reference osisRef="Job.28.7">Job 28:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.7.10">Job 7:10</reference>). <div eID="gen7151" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea4a6806575cd78e489f6e2fec5b385a515df775: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4878"/><div sID="gen7152" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4878"/><hi type="bold">10. seek to please--</hi>"Atone to the poor" (by restoring the property of which they had been robbed by the father) [De Wette]. Better than English Version, "The children" are reduced to the humiliating condition of "seeking the favor of those very poor," whom the father had oppressed. But Umbreit translates as Margin.<div eID="gen7152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his hands--</hi>rather, "their (the children's) hands."<div eID="gen7153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their goods--</hi>the goods of the poor. Righteous retribution! (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7154" type="x-p"/>
entries.34c543db6352ac38afc2e0286be7b1c224c6ed2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4879"/><div sID="gen7155" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4879"/>11. (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.7">Psa 25:7</reference>), so Vulgate. Gesenius has "full of youth"; namely, in the fulness of his youthful strength he shall be laid in the dust. But "bones" plainly alludes to Job's disease, probably to Job's own words (<reference osisRef="Job.19.20">Job 19:20</reference>). Umbreit translates, "full of his secret sins," as in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.8">Psa 90:8</reference>; his secret guilt in his time of seeming righteousness, like secret poison, at last lays him in the dust. The English Version is best. Zophar alludes to Job's own words (<reference osisRef="Job.17.16">Job 17:16</reference>).<div eID="gen7155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with him--</hi>His sin had so pervaded his nature that it accompanies him to the grave: for eternity the sinner cannot get rid of it (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.11">Re 22:11</reference>). <div eID="gen7156" type="x-p"/>
entries.879b15125507f1df4119860dcd85bc9199b478ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4880"/><div sID="gen7157" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4880"/><hi type="bold">12. be--</hi>"taste sweet." Sin's fascination is like poison sweet to the taste, but at last deadly to the vital organs (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.17">Pr 20:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.17">Job 9:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.9.18">18</reference>).<div eID="gen7157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hide ... tongue--</hi>seek to prolong the enjoyment by keeping the sweet morsel long in the mouth (so <reference osisRef="Job.20.13">Job 20:13</reference>). <div eID="gen7158" type="x-p"/>
entries.9749a4f128ab651e01d606b9ce7bd86979727176: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4881"/><div sID="gen7159" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4881"/><hi type="bold">14. turned--</hi>Hebrew denotes a total change into a disagreeable contrary (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jr 2:21</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.10.9">Re 10:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.10.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen7159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gall--</hi>in which the poison of the asp was thought to lie. It rather is contained in a sack in the mouth. Scripture uses popular language, where no moral truth is thereby endangered. <div eID="gen7160" type="x-p"/>
entries.d277ce956c921140e2e0e78544d1586a08dd289d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4882"/><div sID="gen7161" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4882"/>15. He is forced to disgorge his ill-gotten wealth. <div eID="gen7161" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b56a3e8cc7d645a760027c726fadb2fb8d071e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4883"/><div sID="gen7162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4883"/><hi type="bold">16. shall suck--</hi>It shall turn out that he has sucked the poison, &c. <div eID="gen7162" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5f1620f786749225d22ccf669cf6946042165ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4884"/><div sID="gen7163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4884"/><hi type="bold">17. floods--</hi>literally, "stream of floods," plentiful streams flowing with milk, &c. (<reference osisRef="Job.29.6">Job 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.3.17">Ex 3:17</reference>). Honey and butter are more fluid in the East than with us and are poured out from jars. These "rivers" or water brooks are in the sultry East emblems of prosperity. <div eID="gen7163" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9e3b3c5732f17526081385ab5ea9f3533c0d141: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4885"/><div sID="gen7164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4885"/>18. Image from food which is taken away from one before he can swallow it.<div eID="gen7164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">restitution--</hi>(So <reference osisRef="Prov.6.31">Pr 6:31</reference>). The parallelism favors the English Version rather than the translation of Gesenius, "As a possession to be restored in which he rejoices not."<div eID="gen7165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall not rejoice--</hi>His enjoyment of his ill-gotten gains shall then be at an end (<reference osisRef="Job.20.5">Job 20:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7166" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d7beebdf915da89d9e2a58015ddd21850ca5847: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4886"/><div sID="gen7167" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4886"/><hi type="bold">19. oppressed--</hi>whereas he ought to have espoused their cause (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.10">2Ch 16:10</reference>).<div eID="gen7167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forsaken--</hi>left helpless.<div eID="gen7168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house--</hi>thus leaving the poor without shelter (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Is 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.2.2">Mi 2:2</reference>). <div eID="gen7169" type="x-p"/>
entries.fde51f6e166f9a613f546d5c9939946b554418d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4887"/><div sID="gen7170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4887"/>20. Umbreit translates, "His inward parts know no rest" from desires.<div eID="gen7170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his belly--</hi>that is, peace inwardly.<div eID="gen7171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not save--</hi>literally, "not escape with that which," &c., alluding to Job's having been stripped of his all. <div eID="gen7172" type="x-p"/>
entries.b72826c977a91a037dab779a3ef37f748d767c9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4888"/><div sID="gen7173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4888"/><hi type="bold">21. look for--</hi>rather, "because his goods," that is, prosperity shall have no endurance. <div eID="gen7173" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca8736fc62e766d7ed8e5ab9b692fcc0fb15c0c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4889"/><div sID="gen7174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4889"/><hi type="bold">22. shall be--</hi>rather, "he is (feeleth) straitened." The next clause explains in what respect.<div eID="gen7174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wicked--</hi>Rather, "the whole hand of the miserable (whom he had oppressed) cometh upon him"; namely, the sense of his having oppressed the poor, now in turn comes with all its power (hand) on him. This caused his "straitened" feeling even in prosperity. <div eID="gen7175" type="x-p"/>
entries.0eab6f8e4afe7721c22cfa62e571b2a82b07089e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4890"/><div sID="gen7176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4890"/>23. Rather, "God shall cast (may God send) [Umbreit] upon him the fury of His wrath to fill his belly!"<div eID="gen7176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">while ... eating--</hi>rather, "shall rain it upon him for his food!" Fiery rain, that is, lightning (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Psa 11:6</reference>; alluding to Job's misfortune, <reference osisRef="Job.1.16">Job 1:16</reference>). The force of the image is felt by picturing to one's self the opposite nature of a refreshing rain in the desert (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.4">Ex 16:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.9">Psa 68:9</reference>). <div eID="gen7177" type="x-p"/>
entries.77a96b4ef3964841f2ae1c0b68e28a05b5624997: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4891"/><div sID="gen7178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4891"/><hi type="bold">24. steel--</hi>rather, "brass." While the wicked flees from one danger, he falls into a greater one from an opposite quarter [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7178" type="x-p"/>
entries.041da60b064dac9531d6fc5d17677f5e69228ad0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4892"/><div sID="gen7179" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4892"/><hi type="bold">25. It is drawn--</hi>Rather, "He (God) draweth (the sword, <reference osisRef="Josh.5.13">Jos 5:13</reference>) and (no sooner has He done so, than) it cometh out of (that is, passes right through) the (sinner's) body" (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.41">De 32:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.42">42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.9">Eze 21:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.10">10</reference>). The glittering sword is a happy image for lightning.<div eID="gen7179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gall--</hi>that is, his life (<reference osisRef="Job.16.13">Job 16:13</reference>). "Inflicts a deadly wound."<div eID="gen7180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">terrors--</hi>Zophar repeats Bildad's words (<reference osisRef="Job.17.11">Job 17:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.16">Psa 88:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.4">55:4</reference>). <div eID="gen7181" type="x-p"/>
entries.a94218ac89b2b46cc9f777e4ae35eb8df4cbafc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4893"/><div sID="gen7182" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4893"/><hi type="bold">26. All darkness--</hi>that is, every calamity that befalls the wicked shall be hid (in store for him) in His (God's) secret places, or treasures (Jude 13; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.34">De 32:34</reference>).<div eID="gen7182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not blown--</hi>not kindled by man's hands, but by God's (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Is 30:33</reference>; the Septuagint in the Alexandrian Manuscript reads "unquenchable fire," <reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">Mt 3:12</reference>). Tact is shown by the friends in not expressly mentioning, but alluding under color of general cases, to Job's calamities; here (<reference osisRef="Job.1.16">Job 1:16</reference>) Umbreit explains it, wickedness, is a "self-igniting fire"; in it lie the principles of destruction.<div eID="gen7183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ill ... tabernacle--</hi>Every trace of the sinner must be obliterated (<reference osisRef="Job.18.15">Job 18:15</reference>). <div eID="gen7184" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b6dbce3df15e4fa2a6ecc4105635d964f0f2416: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4894"/><div sID="gen7185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4894"/>27. All creation is at enmity with him, and proclaims his guilt, which he would fain conceal. <div eID="gen7185" type="x-p"/>

Ill got--ill gone.<div eID="gen7186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flow away--</hi>like waters that run dry in summer; using Job's own metaphor against himself (<reference osisRef="Job.6.15-Job.6.17">Job 6:15-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.14">2Sa 14:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.4">Mi 1:4</reference>).<div eID="gen7187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his wrath--</hi>God's. <div eID="gen7188" type="x-p"/>

entries.a57411816fae1c31e504525f7d8ee93c9e79900e: <div eID="gen16817" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16818" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16819" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16819" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16818" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16820" type="x-p"/> Zophar answers Job, and largely details the wretchedness of the wicked and the hypocrite; shows that the rejoicing of such is short and transitory, <reference osisRef="Job.20.1-Job.20.9">Job 20:1-9</reference>. That he is punished in his family and in his person, <reference osisRef="Job.20.10-Job.20.14">Job 20:10-14</reference>. That he shall be stripped of his ill-gotten wealth, and shall be in misery, though in the midst of affluence, <reference osisRef="Job.20.15-Job.20.23">Job 20:15-23</reference>. He shall at last die a violent death, and his family and property be finally destroyed, <reference osisRef="Job.20.24-Job.20.29">Job 20:24-29</reference>.
entries.fac6ab32acd942f128cbb9939879234edefa1307: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16821" type="x-p"/> Therefore do my thoughts - It has already been observed that Zophar was the most inveterate of all Job's enemies, for we really must cease to call them friends. He sets no bounds to his invective, and outrages every rule of charity. A man of such a bitter spirit must have been, in general, very unhappy. With him Job is, by insinuation, every thing that is base, vile, and hypocritical. Mr. Good translates this verse thus: "Whither would my tumult transport me? And how far my agitation within me?" This is all the modesty that appears in Zophar's discourse. He acknowledges that he is pressed by the impetuosity of his spirit to reply to Job's self-vindication. The original is variously translated, but the sense is as above. <div eID="gen16821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16822" type="x-p"/> For this I make haste - ובעבור חושי בי ubaabur chushi bi, there is sensibility in me, and my feelings provoke me to reply.
entries.05cc78ec30af2c8271a6d8338c65194cc4ac756c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16823" type="x-p"/> I have heard the check of my reproach - Some suppose that Zophar quotes the words of Job, and that some words should be supplied to indicate this meaning; e.g., "I have heard (sayest thou) the check or charge of my reproach?" Or it may refer to what Job says of Zophar and his companions, <reference osisRef="Job.19.2">Job 19:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.19.3">Job 19:3</reference> : How long will ye vex may soul - these ten times have ye reproached me. Zophar therefore assumes his old ground, and retracts nothing of what he had said. Like many of his own complexion in the present day, he was determined to believe that his judgment was infallible, and that he could not err.
entries.1b77978e90356a62ef65e329e64b4873e7f09171: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16824" type="x-p"/> Knowest thou not this of old - This is a maxim as ancient as the world; it began with the first man: A wicked man shall triumph but a short time; God will destroy the proud doer. <div eID="gen16824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16825" type="x-p"/> Since man was placed upon earth - Literally, since Adam was placed on the earth; that is, since the fall, wickedness and hypocrisy have existed; but they have never triumphed long. Thou hast lately been expressing confidence in reference to a general judgment; but such is thy character, that thou hast little reason to anticipate with any joy the decisions of that day.
entries.ae752d7a63607dd261c23d2fb603c5da3ad8cc73: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16826" type="x-p"/> Though his excellency mount up to the heavens - Probably referring to the original state of Adam, of whose fall he appears to have spoken, <reference osisRef="Job.20.4">Job 20:4</reference>. He was created in the image of God; but by his sin against his Maker he fell into wretchedness, misery, death, and destruction.
entries.c44584613c641f66225e93fc43b2dfd44dff6aba: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16827" type="x-p"/> He shall perish for ever - He is dust, and shall return to the dust from which he was taken. Zophar here hints his disbelief in that doctrine, the resurrection of the body, which Job had so solemnly asserted in the preceding chapter. Or he might have been like some in the present day, who believe that the wicked shall be annihilated, and the bodies of the righteous only be raised from the dead; but I know of no scripture by which such a doctrine is confirmed. <div eID="gen16827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16828" type="x-p"/> Like his own dung - His reputation shall be abominable, and his putrid carcass shall resemble his own excrement. A speech that partakes as much of the malevolence as of the asperity of Zophar's spirit.
entries.57414c52a2b73c2ddb7b1acc1a1911473d654aed: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16829" type="x-p"/> He shall fly away as a dream - Instead of rising again from corruption, as thou hast asserted, (<reference osisRef="Job.19.26">Job 19:26</reference>), with a new body, his flesh shall rot in the earth, and his spirit be dissipated like a vapor; and, like a vision of the night, nothing shall remain but the bare impression that such a creature had once existed, but shall appear no more for ever.
entries.e8e142013eb6e16aea73bde60a1c30138d0ecc1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16830" type="x-p"/> His children shall seek to please the poor - They shall be reduced to the lowest degree of poverty and want, so as to be obliged to become servants to the poor. Cursed be Ham, a servant of servants shall he be. There are cases where the poor actually serve the poor; and this is the lowest or most abject state of poverty. <div eID="gen16830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16831" type="x-p"/> His hands shall restore their goods - He shall be obliged to restore the goods that he has taken by violence. Mr. Good translates: His branches shall be involved in his iniquity; i.e., his children shall suffer on his account. "His own hands shall render to himself the evil that he has done to others." - Calmet. The clause is variously translated.
entries.3f05f9b76188ba869886d3786e8ae8011a977dd7: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16832" type="x-p"/> His bones are full of the sin of his youth - Our translators have followed the Vulgate, Ossa ejus implebuntur vitiis adolescentiae ejus; "his bones shall be filled with the sins of his youth." The Syriac and Arabic have, his bones are full of marrow; and the Targum is to the same sense. At first view it might appear that Zophar refers to those infirmities in old age, which are the consequences of youthful vices and irregularities. עלומו alumau, which we translate his youth, may be rendered his hidden things; as if he had said, his secret vices bring down his strength to the dust. For this rendering Rosenmuller contends, and several other German critics. Mr. Good contends for the same.
entries.37f87862f1d0d0101b9fdb7f64a0f82c711fb7c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16833" type="x-p"/> Though wickedness be sweet in his mouth - This seems to refer to the secret sins mentioned above. <div eID="gen16833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16834" type="x-p"/> Hide it under his tongue - This and the four following verses contain an allegory; and the reference is to a man who, instead of taking wholesome food, takes what is poisonous, and is so delighted with it because it is sweet, that he rolls it under his tongue, and will scarcely let it down into his stomach, he is so delighted with the taste; "he spares it, and forsakes it not, but keeps it still within his mouth," <reference osisRef="Job.20.13">Job 20:13</reference>. "But when he swallows it, it is turned to the gall of asps within him," <reference osisRef="Job.20.14">Job 20:14</reference>, which shall corrode and torture his bowels.
entries.b8ad023eedc226acf60e1624883b2162c187c95b: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16835" type="x-p"/> He shall vomit them up again - This is also an allusion to an effect of most ordinary poisons; they occasion a nausea, and often excruciating vomiting; nature striving to eject what it knows, if retained, will be its bane.
entries.1f08a2e4ce204bf1d30ce61ebabd810dcc0e7b61: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16836" type="x-p"/> He shall suck the poison of asps - That delicious morsel, that secret, easily-besetting sin, so palatable, and so pleasurable, shall act on the life of his soul, as the poison of asps would do on the life of his body. The poison is called the gall of asps, it being anciently supposed that the poison of serpents consists in their gall, which is thought to be copiously exuded when those animals are enraged; as it has been often seen that their bite is not poisonous when they are not angry. Pliny, in speaking of the various parts of animals, Hist. Nat. lib. xi., c. 37, states, from this circumstance, that in the gall, the poison of serpents consists; ne quis miretur id (fel) venenum esse serpentum. And in lib. xxviii., c. 9, he ranks the gall of horses among the poisons: Damnatur (fel) equinum tantum inter venena. We see, therefore, that the gall was considered to be the source whence the poison of serpents was generated, not only in Arabia, but also in Italy.
entries.5308aa3dea96c401c4abfd17a2e1214cabba499c: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16837" type="x-p"/> He shall not see the rivers - Mr. Good has the following judicious note on this passage: "Honey and butter are the common results of a rich, well-watered pasturage, offering a perpetual banquet of grass to kine, and of nectar to bees; and thus loading the possessor with the most luscious luxuries of pastoral life, peculiarly so before the discovery of the means of obtaining sugar. The expression appears to have been proverbial; and is certainly used here to denote a very high degree of temporal prosperity." See also <reference osisRef="Job.29.6">Job 29:6</reference>. To the Hebrews such expressions were quite familiar. See <reference osisRef="Exo.3.8">Exo 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.13.5">Exo 13:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.33.3">Exo 33:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.32">2Kgs 18:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.31.20">Deu 31:20</reference>, and elsewhere. The Greek and Roman writers abound in such images. Milk and honey were such delicacies with the ancients, that Pindar compares his song to them for its smoothness and sweetness: - Χαιρε Φιλος. Εγω τοδε τοι Πεμπω μεμιγμενον μελι λευκῳ Συν γαλακτι· κιρναμενα δ' εερς' αμφεπει πομ' αοιδιμον, Αιολισιν εν πνοαισιν αυλων. <div eID="gen16837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16838" type="x-p"/> Pind. Nem. iii., ver. 133. "Hail, friend! to thee I tune my song; <div eID="gen16838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16839" type="x-p"/> For thee its mingled sweets prepare; <div eID="gen16839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16840" type="x-p"/> Mellifluous accents pour along; <div eID="gen16840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16841" type="x-p"/> Verse, pure as milk, to thee I bear; <div eID="gen16841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16842" type="x-p"/> On all thy actions falls the dew of praise; <div eID="gen16842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16843" type="x-p"/> Pierian draughts thy thirst of fame assuage, <div eID="gen16843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16844" type="x-p"/> And breathing flutes thy songs of triumph raise." <div eID="gen16844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16845" type="x-p"/> J. B. C. <div eID="gen16845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16846" type="x-p"/> Qui te, Pollio, amat, veniat, quo te quoque gaudet; <div eID="gen16846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16847" type="x-p"/> Mella fluant illi, ferat et rubus asper amomum. <div eID="gen16847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16848" type="x-p"/> Virg. Ecl. iii., ver. 88. "Who Pollio loves, and who his muse admires; <div eID="gen16848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16849" type="x-p"/> Let Pollio's fortune crown his full desires <div eID="gen16849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16850" type="x-p"/> Let myrrh, instead of thorn, his fences fill; <div eID="gen16850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16851" type="x-p"/> And showers of honey from his oaks distil!" <div eID="gen16851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16852" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen16852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16853" type="x-p"/> Ovid, describing the golden age, employs the same image: - <div eID="gen16853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16854" type="x-p"/> Flumina jam lactis, jam flumina nectaris ibant; <div eID="gen16854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16855" type="x-p"/> Flavaque de viridi stillabant ilice mella. <div eID="gen16855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16856" type="x-p"/> Metam. lib. i., ver. 3. "Floods were with milk, and floods with nectar, fill'd; <div eID="gen16856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16857" type="x-p"/> And honey from the sweating oak distill'd." <div eID="gen16857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16858" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen16858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16859" type="x-p"/> Horace employs a similar image in nearly the same words: - <div eID="gen16859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16860" type="x-p"/> Mella cava manant ex ilice, montibus altis; <div eID="gen16860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16861" type="x-p"/> Levis crepante lympha desilit pede. <div eID="gen16861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16862" type="x-p"/> Epod. xvi., ver. 46. "From hollow oaks, where honey'd streams distil, <div eID="gen16862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16863" type="x-p"/> And bounds with noisy foot the pebbled rill." <div eID="gen16863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16864" type="x-p"/> Francis. <div eID="gen16864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16865" type="x-p"/> Job employs the same metaphor, <reference osisRef="Job.29.6">Job 29:6</reference> : - <div eID="gen16865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16866" type="x-p"/> When I washed my steps with butter, <div eID="gen16866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16867" type="x-p"/> And the rock poured out to me rivers of oil. <div eID="gen16867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16868" type="x-p"/> Isaiah, also, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.22">Isa 7:22</reference>, uses the same when describing the produce of a heifer and two ewes: - <div eID="gen16868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16869" type="x-p"/> From the plenty of milk that they shall produce, <div eID="gen16869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16870" type="x-p"/> He shall eat butter: butter and honey shall he eat, <div eID="gen16870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16871" type="x-p"/> Whosoever is left in the midst of the land. <div eID="gen16871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16872" type="x-p"/> And Joel, <reference osisRef="Joe.3.18">Joe 3:18</reference> : - <div eID="gen16872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16873" type="x-p"/> And it shall come to pass in that day, <div eID="gen16873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16874" type="x-p"/> The mountains shall drop down new wine, <div eID="gen16874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16875" type="x-p"/> And the hills shall flow with milk; <div eID="gen16875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16876" type="x-p"/> And all the rivers of Judah shall flow with waters. <div eID="gen16876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16877" type="x-p"/> These expressions denote fertility and abundance; and are often employed to point out the excellence of the promised land, which is frequently denominated a land flowing with milk and honey: and even the superior blessings of the Gospel are thus characterized, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.1">Isa 51:1</reference>.
entries.8d16f49123d531f65a06b0afde084bef70b1f512: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16878" type="x-p"/> That which he laboureth for shall he restore - I prefer here the reading of the Arabic, which is also supported by the Syriac, and is much nearer to the Hebrew text than the common version. He shall return to labor, but he shall not eat; he shall toil, and not be permitted to enjoy the fruit of his labor. The whole of this verse Mr. Good thus translates: - "To labor shall he return, but he shall not eat. <div eID="gen16878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16879" type="x-p"/> A dearth his recompense: yea, nothing shall he taste." <div eID="gen16879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16880" type="x-p"/> It may be inquired how Mr. Good arrives at this meaning. It is by considering the word יעלס yaalos, which we translate he shall rejoice, as the Arabic (Arabic) alasa, "he ate, drank, tasted;" and the word כהיל kehil, which we make a compound word, keeheyl, "according to substance," to be the pure Arabic word (Arabic) kahala, "it was fruitless," applied to a year of dearth: hence kahlan, "a barren year." Conceiving these two to be pure Arabic words, for which he seems to have sufficient authority, he renders תמורתו temuratho, his recompense, as in <reference osisRef="Job.15.31">Job 15:31</reference>, and not restitution, as here. The general meaning is, He shall labor and toil, but shall not reap, for God shall send on his land blasting and mildew. Houbigant translates the verse thus: Reddet labore partum; neque id absumet; copiosae fuerunt mercaturae ejus, sed illis non fruetur. "He shall restore what he gained by labor, nor shall he consume it; his merchandises were abundant, but he shall not enjoy them." O, how doctors disagree! Old Coverdale gives a good sense, which is no unfrequent thing with this venerable translator: - <div eID="gen16880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16881" type="x-p"/> But laboure shal he, and yet have nothinge to eate; great travayle shal he make for riches, but he shal not enjoye them.
entries.bcc13e1eef6c72667715e46d776db67064253fcb: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16882" type="x-p"/> He hath oppressed and hath forsaken the poor - Literally, He hath broken in pieces the forsaken of the poor; כי רצץ עזב דלים ki ritstsats azab dallim. The poor have fled from famine, and left their children behind them; and this hard-hearted wretch, meaning Job all the while, has suffered them to perish, when he might have saved them alive. <div eID="gen16882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16883" type="x-p"/> He hath violently taken away a house which he builded not - Or rather, He hath thrown down a house, and hath not rebuilt it. By neglecting or destroying the forsaken orphans of the poor, mentioned above, he has destroyed a house, (a family), while he might, by helping the wretched, have preserved the family from becoming extinct.
entries.e05ca309e3c5b0858b59e0e15aa5b561b91bd00d: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16884" type="x-p"/> Surely he shall not feel quietness in his belly - I have already remarked that the word בטן beten, which we translate belly, often means in the sacred Scriptures the whole of the human trunk; the regions of the thorax and abdomen, with their contents; the heart, lungs, liver, etc., and consequently all the thoughts, purposes, and inclinations of the mind, of which those viscera were supposed to be the functionaries. The meaning seems to be, "He shall never be satisfied; he shall have an endless desire after secular good, and shall never be able to obtain what he covets."
entries.d8d23ce29f6be884d259ee6ee686ff490c33f7ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16885" type="x-p"/> There shall none of his meat be left - Coverdale translates thus: He devoured so gredily, that he left nothinge behynde, therefore his goodes shal not prospere. He shall be stripped of every thing.
entries.2059961a2bd09ab232ba4b6f10303edb87465d98: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16886" type="x-p"/> In the fullness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits - This is a fine saying, and few of the menders of Job's text have been able to improve the version. It is literally true of every great, rich, wicked man; he has no God, and anxieties and perplexities torment him, notwithstanding he has his portion in this life. <div eID="gen16886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16887" type="x-p"/> Every hand of the wicked shall come upon him - All kinds of misery shall be his portion. Coverdale translates: Though he had plenteousnesse of every thinge, yet was he poore; and, therefore, he is but a wretch on every syde.
entries.7781b5ae9277ed9d40fc452d8c1efe5a91d08802: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen16887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16888" type="x-p"/> When he is about to fill his belly - Here seems a plain allusion to the lustings of the children of Israel in the desert. God showered down quails upon them, and showered down his wrath while the flesh was in their mouth. The allusion is too plain to be mistaken; and this gives some countenance to the bishop of Killala's version of <reference osisRef="Job.20.20">Job 20:20</reference> - "Because he acknowledged not the quail in his stomach, <div eID="gen16888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16889" type="x-p"/> In the midst of his delight he shall not escape." <div eID="gen16889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16890" type="x-p"/> That שלו, which we translate quietness, means a quail, also the history of the Hebrews' lustings, <reference osisRef="Exo.16.2-Exo.16.11">Exo 16:2-11</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Num.11.31-Num.11.35">Num 11:31-35</reference>, sufficiently proves. Let the reader mark all the expressions here, <reference osisRef="Job.20.20-Job.20.23">Job 20:20-23</reference>, and compare them with <reference osisRef="Num.11.31-Num.11.35">Num 11:31-35</reference>, and he will probably be of opinion that Zophar has that history immediately in view, which speaks of the Hebrews' murmurings for bread and flesh, and the miraculous showers of manna and quails, and the judgments that fell on them for their murmurings. Let us compare a few passages: - <reference osisRef="Job.20.20">Job 20:20</reference>. He shall not feel quietness - שלו selav, the quail. "He shall not save of that which he desired." <reference osisRef="Job.20.21">Job 20:21</reference> : "There shall none of his meat be left." <reference osisRef="Exo.16.19">Exo 16:19</reference> : "Let no man leave of it till the morning." <reference osisRef="Job.20.22">Job 20:22</reference>. In the fullness of his sufficiency, he shall be in straits - <reference osisRef="Exo.16.20">Exo 16:20</reference> : "But some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms and stank." <reference osisRef="Job.20.23">Job 20:23</reference>. When he is about to fill his belly, God shall cast the fury of his wrath upon him, and shall rain it upon him while he is eating - <reference osisRef="Num.11.33">Num 11:33</reference> : "And while the flesh was yet between their teeth, ere it was chewed, the wrath of the Lord was kindled against the people, and the Lord smote the people with a very great plague." <reference osisRef="Psa.78.26-Psa.78.30">Psa 78:26-30</reference> : "He rained flesh upon them as dust, and feathered fowls like as the sand of the sea: so they did eat and were filled-but, while the meat was in their mouth, the wrath of God came upon them," etc. These show to what Zophar refers.
entries.0920175f18bb49c3f5ed1a1c344e66719d7febf6: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen16890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16891" type="x-p"/> He shall flee from the iron weapon - Or, "Though he should flee from the iron armor, the brazen bow should strike him through." So that yf he fle the yron weapens, he shal be shott with the stele bow - Coverdale. That is, he shall most certainly perish: all kinds of deaths await him.
entries.808cffc880f691016d1ae5f7a3d9ff1e3e525fd4: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen16891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16892" type="x-p"/> It is drawn, and cometh out - This refers to archery: The arrow is drawn out of the sheaf or quiver, and discharged from the bow against its mark, and pierces the vitals, and passes through the body. So Coverdale - The arowe shal be taken forth, and go out at his backe.
entries.bb4637d1430580b1d760747cdc00529e985647b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen16892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16893" type="x-p"/> A fire not blown shall consume him - As Zophar is here showing that the wicked cannot escape from the Divine judgments; so he points out the different instruments which God employs for their destruction. The wrath of God - any secret or supernatural curse. The iron weapon - the spear or such like. The bow, and its swift-flying arrow. <div eID="gen16893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16894" type="x-p"/> Darkness - deep horror and perplexity. A fire not blown - a supernatural fire; lightning: such as fell on Korah, and his company, to whose destruction there is probably here an allusion: hence the words, It shall go ill with him who is left in his tabernacle. "And the Lord spake unto Moses and Aaron, Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment. Get ye up from about the tabernacle of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. Depart from the tents of these wicked men. There came out a fire from the Lord and consumed the two hundred and fifty men that offered incense;" <reference osisRef="Num.16.20">Num 16:20</reference>, etc.
entries.71685e570e78a465654db30d750775a84589c9c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen16894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16895" type="x-p"/> The heaven shall reveal his iniquity; and the earth shall rise up against him - Another allusion, if I mistake not, to the destruction of Korah and his company. The heaven revealed their iniquity; God declared out of heaven his judgment of their rebellion. "And the glory of the Lord appeared unto all the congregation;" <reference osisRef="Num.16.20">Num 16:20</reference>, etc. And then the earth rose up against them. "The ground clave asunder that was under them, and the earth opened her mouth and swallowed them up; and they went down alive into the pit, and the earth closed upon them;" <reference osisRef="Num.16.31-Num.16.33">Num 16:31-33</reference>.
entries.b19b44b05ee06eeca4b8aac0e018511571e9b2c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen16895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16896" type="x-p"/> The increase of his house shall depart, and his goods shall flow away in the day of his wrath - A farther allusion to the punishment of the rebellious company of Korah, who not only perished themselves, but their houses also, and their goods. <reference osisRef="Num.16.32">Num 16:32</reference>. These examples were all in point, on the ground assumed by Zophar; and such well-attested facts would not be passed over by him, had he known the record of them; and that he did know it, alludes to it, and quotes the very circumstances, is more than probable.
entries.b4e0f2b928ed63d38af9de624b54b36a1c1feb16: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen16896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16897" type="x-p"/> This is the portion - As God has dealt with the murmuring Israelites, and with the rebellious sons of Korah, so will he deal with those who murmur against the dispensations of his providence, and rebel against his authority. Instead of an earthly portion, and an ecclesiastical heritage, such as Korah, Dathan, and Abiram sought; they shall have fire from God to scorch them, and the earth to swallow them up.
